Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male 
Age: 14 years
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Discharge Diagnosis: Dermoid cyst of conus medullaris

Hospital Course:

The patient was initially diagnosed with tuberculosis of the spine by a district registered medical officer and started on antituberculous therapy. However, the patient's condition worsened, and he was transferred to our tertiary care hospital. He complained of lower back pain, weakness, and numbness in his lower limbs. The patient's higher mental function was normal, and his cranial nerves were intact.

Upon further assessment, a reduced bulk of the flexor group of both lower limbs, hypotonia on the left side, grade 3/5 power in both the lower limbs, and areflexia bilaterally were observed. Sensory examination revealed hypoesthesia and decreased light touch and pinprick sensation in the L5/L4 dermatomes of his right lower limb. The sacral dermatomal sensations at S1/S2 levels were also impaired.

Radiological investigations showed a focal, well-defined space-occupying lesion measuring 1.50×0.6cm2, and abnormal signal intensity within the spinal canal, which was intradural as well as intramedullary in nature, compressing the conus medullaris at the D12 and L1 level. The lesion was heterogeneously intense, localized, and well demarcated. The tumor was hypointense at the T1-weighted frequency with a hyperintense signal area at the caudal end.

Surgical resection was performed through a posterior midline linear incision at the D12 and L1 level. The spinal cord was seen to be compressed and overdistended due to an intrinsic lesion, and myelotomy was performed. A well-demarcated, unilocular, grayish white intradural, intramedullary cyst was found involving the conus medullaris and extending from D12 and L1. The cyst was evacuated and near-total excision was done from the neuronal tissue. A histopathological examination revealed the diagnosis of dermoid cyst, which was confirmed by the presence of aggregates of keratinocytes along with keratin flakes.

Post-surgery, the patient showed gradual improvement in motor power to grade 4/5 in both lower limbs and restoration of light touch and pinprick sensation. After a month of follow-up, there were no abnormal neurological sequelae, and the patient was able to mobilize and walk with support.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient has been discharged on [REDACTED]. Please follow up with your primary care doctor or neurologist for further consultation. In case of any recurrence of symptoms, please return to our hospital immediately.

Discharge Diagnosis: A non-cancerous sac filled with skin-like tissue near the lower end of the spinal cord

Hospital Course:

The patient was first told he had a spine infection called tuberculosis by a local doctor. He was given medicine for that illness. But the patient got worse, so he was moved to our hospital. He had pain in his lower back. He also had weakness and numbness in both legs. The patient's thinking and memory were normal. The nerves in his head and face were working fine.

Doctors found that the muscles in both lower legs had gotten smaller. The left side had loose muscle tone. Both legs had weak strength, rated 3 out of 5. Reflexes were missing in both legs. The patient had reduced feeling in parts of his right leg. He could not feel light touch or sharp pokes as well as normal. Feeling was also reduced in the area around his buttocks and upper thighs.

Scans showed a small, clearly shaped growth measuring about 1.5 by 0.6 centimeters. This growth was inside the spinal canal and pressing on the lower end of the spinal cord. The growth was located at the middle-to-lower back area. It had clear edges and different shades on the scan images.

Doctors did surgery through a straight cut in the middle of the back. They found the spinal cord was being squeezed by a growth inside it. They made a small opening in the spinal cord covering. Inside, they found a grayish-white sac with one pocket. This sac was growing in the lower end of the spinal cord. The doctors drained the sac and removed almost all of it. Lab tests showed the sac was a harmless cyst lined with skin cells.

After surgery, the patient slowly got stronger. Leg strength improved to 4 out of 5. Feeling for light touch and sharp pokes came back. One month later, the patient had no nerve problems. He could move around and walk with help.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient has been discharged on [REDACTED]. Please follow up with your primary care doctor or brain and nerve specialist for further consultation. In case of any return of symptoms, please return to our hospital immediately.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of right flank pain, low-grade fever, nausea, anorexia, and unintentional weight loss. Upon physical examination, she was found to have tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant and epigastric regions. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed a well-defined complex solid-cystic mass in the neck of the pancreas. Additionally, a routine chest X-ray revealed suspicious mediastinal lymphadenopathy. CT scans of the chest and abdomen were subsequently sought that revealed mediastinal lymphadenopathy, bilateral pleural effusions, and a 4.5 x 5.5 cm mass in the neck of the pancreas with mixed solid and cystic features.

Further investigations revealed multiple non-caseating granulomas, negative flow cytometry and special stains for microorganisms, and elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level. These findings eventually led to the diagnosis of sarcoidosis in this patient. A CT-guided biopsy of the pancreatic mass revealed polygonal epithelial cells with characteristic pseudopapillary changes, leading to the diagnosis of pseudopapillary tumor (Frantz tumor) of the pancreas. Special stains including vimentin and beta-catenin were positive, thus confirming our diagnosis.

The patient underwent a Whipple pancreaticoduodenectomy for her pancreatic mass and she recovered well post-operatively. On discharge, she was in a stable hemodynamic condition.

1. Continue taking prescribed medications as directed by your healthcare provider.
2. Follow-up with your healthcare provider for routine monitoring and management of your medical condition.
3. If you experience any symptoms or concerns, contact your healthcare provider immediately.

A 66-year-old female patient was admitted to the Department of Periodontics, M. S. Ramaiah Dental College and Hospital, Bangalore, with the complaint of burning sensation in the gums and bleeding gums for the past one month.

Medical History:
The patient had no relevant drug history or significant medical history. She had not received any dental treatment before.

Examination Findings:
On extra oral examination, the patient had some obvious skin lesions on the scalp and a hyperkeratotic plaque behind her left ear. Intra oral examination of gingiva revealed reddish marginal, attached gingiva and interdental papilla in both maxillary and mandibular anterior region with desquamation of epithelium present in certain regions.

Diagnosis:
Based on the clinical and histopathologic features, the lesion was suggestive of discoid lupus erythematosus.

Treatment:
Hand scaling was performed as gently as possible in order to minimize tissue disruption. Soft tooth brush and mouth rise (chlorhexidine 0.12%) was recommended. Triamcinolone acteonide oral paste was advised to apply two to three times per day.

Follow-up:
The patient was recalled for follow-up and maintenance.

Hospital Course:
A 66-year-old female patient came to the gum care department at M. S. Ramaiah Dental College and Hospital in Bangalore. She had a burning feeling in her gums and bleeding gums for the past month.

Medical History:
The patient was not taking any medicines and had no major health problems. She had never had dental treatment before.

The dentist looked at the outside of the patient's face and body. The patient had some skin patches on her scalp. She also had a thick, rough patch of skin behind her left ear. The dentist then looked inside the patient's mouth. The gums around the upper and lower front teeth were red. This included the gums at the edges, the gums attached to the teeth, and the gums between the teeth. In some areas, the top layer of gum tissue was peeling off.

Diagnosis:
Based on what the dentist saw and lab test results, the patient likely has discoid lupus erythematosus. This is a condition where the body's defense system attacks its own skin and gum tissue.

Treatment:
The dentist gently cleaned the teeth to remove buildup. This was done carefully to avoid hurting the gums. The patient was told to use a soft toothbrush and rinse with chlorhexidine 0.12 percent mouthwash. The patient was also told to apply triamcinolone acetonide paste inside the mouth two to three times per day. This paste helps reduce soreness and swelling.

Follow-up:
The patient was asked to come back for check-up visits and ongoing care.

The 50-year-old male agriculturist was referred to our hospital for the management of acute crisis. The patient was admitted with a history of intermittent epigastric pain. He had undergone exploratory laparotomy for generalized peritonitis and duodenal perforation two days ago at a general hospital.

The patient had renal failure with hypokalemia and complained of severe abdominal pain and decreased urine output for the last 5 days at the time of admission in the general hospital. After surgery, the patient had puffiness of face and breathlessness, severe metabolic acidosis, hypotension, altered sensorium, and fever. The patient was put on ventilatory support and antibiotics (aztreonam, metronidazole, and intravenous fluids) considering bacterial peritonitis. Despite all these measures, the patient's condition deteriorated.

Peripheral blood examination showed normocytic normochromic anemia with elongated cells, stomatocytes and target cells. The results of laboratory examinations were as follows: Neutrophilic leucocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated ESR, elevated serum urea and creatinine levels, hypernatremia, hyperkalemia, elevated total bilirubin and conjugated bilirubin. Ultra-sonography revealed mild parenchymal renal disease, minimal perisplenic collection in the abdomen, and dilated intrahepatic biliary ducts. Urine microscopy showed 2-3 pus cells/HPF. Peritoneal fluid Gram stain smear showed occasional pus cells with few budding yeast cells and many barrel-shaped arthroconidia. Blood culture was sterile after 24 hours.

Peritoneal fluid culture was positive for Trichosporon beigelii. On the basis of these tests, the infection was treated as per standard medical protocol. Despite the treatment, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and hence, he was referred for the management of acute crisis.

Given the severity of the patient's condition, he will receive ongoing supportive care. Further treatment will be provided as necessary.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with Trichosporon beigelii infection, which was treated during his hospital stay.

The patient will receive ongoing follow-up care to ensure that he receives the necessary treatment. Any follow-up care instructions will be provided during subsequent visits.

Hospital Course Summary:

History of Present Illness:
The patient, a previously healthy 3.5-year-old male, was admitted with complaints of weakness and pallor lasting for five days. The patient had a three-day history of diarrhea two weeks before the admission. A physical examination revealed jaundice, pallor, and splenomegaly. The initial laboratory investigation showed low hemoglobin levels, and polychromasia and spherocytes were observed in the peripheral blood film. The patient was diagnosed with the warm type of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA).

Hospital Course:
Erythrocyte transfusion was administered, followed by intravenous methylprednisolone. The patient showed an excellent hematological response to the treatment. Oral prednisolone was used for four weeks, followed by a slow taper during the next five months. The patient experienced a relapse after an upper respiratory infection, and prednisolone was restarted with a good hematological response. The dose of prednisolone was reduced, resulting in hematological deterioration. Azathioprine was initiated, but there was a slight hematological deterioration. Rituximab was initiated after informed written consent and given in four weekly doses. The patient showed a stable response two months after the initiation of rituximab. The DAT became negative 12 months later, and the patient remains disease-free without relapses, three years after the first presentation.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Warm type of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA)

Discharge Medication:
None

Discharge Condition:
Stable

Follow-up Appointments:
The patient is advised to follow-up with the appropriate specialists as needed.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow a healthy lifestyle and diet and rest as needed.

The patient was diagnosed with the warm type of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) and responded well to various treatments, including erythrocyte transfusion, intravenous methylprednisolone, oral prednisolone, azathioprine, and rituximab. The patient has healed well after surgery. The patient should schedule regular visits with the regular doctor. No other tests are needed. No medications have been prescribed at discharge.

Physical Examination: On extraoral examination, facial asymmetry was noted in the lower left facial region, but there was no evidence of any regional lymphadenopathy. Computed tomography (CT) scans confirmed the presence of aggressive bony resorption of the lower left jaw starting from the premolar region and extending well into the mandibular ramus. Histopathological analysis of a biopsy specimen confirmed an aggressive CGCG.

Hospital Course: The patient underwent surgical excision and reconstruction using a submental island flap, under general anesthesia. The surgical procedure involved extraoral and intraoral approach to excise the lesion completely and a submental island flap for reconstruction. The patient was discharged without any complications.

Follow-up: In subsequent follow-ups, until one year, no evidence of recurrence was observed clinically as well as radiographically. The donor site healed uneventfully with minimal scars, which was present away from aesthetically visible regions of the face.

Summary: A 50-year-old female patient presented with an intraoral swelling at the left mandible for six months and was diagnosed with an aggressive CGCG. The patient underwent surgical excision and reconstruction using a submental island flap, under general anesthesia. The patient was discharged without any complications, and subsequent follow-ups showed no evidence of recurrence.

This bone loss went from the small back teeth area into the back part of the jawbone. A small tissue sample was taken and looked at under a microscope.

Follow-up: At checkup visits over the next year, there were no signs that the growth came back. This was checked by looking in the mouth and taking x-rays. The area under the chin where tissue was taken healed well with very little scarring. The small scar is not in a part of the face that people easily see.

Summary: A 50-year-old female patient came in with swelling inside the mouth on the left side of the lower jaw for six months. The patient had surgery to remove the growth and rebuild the area using skin and tissue from under the chin. The patient was asleep under general anesthesia during the procedure.
